I think it will be better to actually consolidate into just one workflow.

Yeah, it looks like it is a trade-off between - quickly rerunning failing workflows and quickly cancelling workflows.

I think there are ways to auto-cancel workflows when there is a new push and thus a new run for the same workflow initiated. For example, just googling I found this https://stackoverflow.com/a/67939898.

Looking at the Simplifier pass, it changes 

```fortran
program expr2
implicit none

integer :: x = (2+3)*5

end program
```
to
```fortran
program expr2
implicit none

integer :: x
x = (2+3)*5

end program
```

Thus, I believe we are moving towards the idea that `parameter must have a value` and `a non-parameter must not have an initial value, but rather be assigned its initial value`. I could very well be incorrect here and, ideally we should verify this with someone who has worked on the simplifier pass before.

This PR adds a docker file to support building a docker image for `lfortran`. The built docker image is currently uploaded here https://hub.docker.com/repository/docker/ubaidsh/lfortran-build/general. 

### Test plan

First install docker https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/.

#### To test the docker image

- run the image interactively `docker run -it ubaidsh/lfortran-build`
- one can find `lfortran` in `/app/bin/lfortran`

#### To generate the docker image.

```console
docker build -t lfortran-build .
```

towards https://github.com/lfortran/lfortran/issues/2478

This PR adds a docker file to support building a docker image for `lfortran`. The built docker image is currently uploaded here https://hub.docker.com/repository/docker/ubaidsh/lfortran-build/general. 

### Test plan

First install docker https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/.

#### To test the docker image

- run the image interactively `docker run -it ubaidsh/lfortran-build`
- one can find `lfortran` in `/app/bin/lfortran`

#### To generate the docker image

towards https://github.com/lfortran/lfortran/issues/2478

### Test plan

First install docker https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/.

#### To test the docker image

- run the image interactively `docker run -it ubaidsh/lfortran-build`
- one can find `lfortran` in `/app/bin/lfortran`

#### To generate the docker image

### Test plan

First install docker https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/.

#### To test the docker image

- run the image interactively `docker run -it ubaidsh/lfortran-build`
- one can find `lfortran` in `/app/bin/lfortran`

#### To generate the docker image

- run `docker build -t lfortran-build .` from the root directory of `lfortran` towards https://github.com/lfortran/lfortran/issues/2478

This PR adds a docker file to support building a docker image for `lfortran`. The built docker image is currently uploaded here https://hub.docker.com/repository/docker/ubaidsh/lfortran-build/general. 

### Test plan

First install docker https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/.

#### To test the docker image

- run the image interactively `docker run -it ubaidsh/lfortran-build`
- one can find `lfortran` in `/app/bin/lfortran`

#### To generate the docker image

- run `docker build -t lfortran-build .` from the root directory of `lfortran` ### Test plan

First install docker https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/.

#### To test the docker image

- run the image interactively `docker run -it ubaidsh/lfortran-build`
- one can find `lfortran` in `/app/bin/lfortran`

#### To generate the docker image

```console
% lfortran_in_main integration_tests/parameter_08.f90 --backend fortran
   1.13508582    
ERROR STOP
```

If we see the generated fortran code:

```console
% lfortran_in_main integration_tests/parameter_08.f90 --show-fortran
program parameter_08
implicit none
real(4), dimension(4), parameter :: a = [0.841471, 0.909297, 0.141120, -0.756802]
real(4), dimension(4), parameter :: b = [0.745624, 0.789072, 0.140652, -0.686600]
real(4), dimension(4), parameter :: c = [0.734665, 0.704504, 0.990125, 0.773406]
....
```

The `cos` gets optimized with the compile-time value.

So, we should enable or add a test that tests the `cos` function for the `fortran` backend.

real(4) :: x
real(8) :: y

y = 7.20000000_8

print *, y

end program

   7.19999981    
   7.2000000000000002 
```

program compile_time
implicit none
integer, parameter :: N = 65535
integer, parameter :: sp = kind(1.0)
integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.d0)
real(dp), parameter :: pi = 2*asin(1._dp)
real(dp), parameter :: a = 0, b = pi
real(dp), parameter :: dx = (b-a)/N
integer :: i
real(dp), parameter :: X(*) = [(sin(a+(b-a)*i/N), i = 1, N)]
real(dp), parameter :: S = sum(X)*dx
logical, parameter :: l = S < 2
real(kind=merge(sp, dp, l)) :: y
if (kind(y) == sp) then
    print *, "true"
else
    print *, "false"
end if
print *, S
end program
```

It seems for the runtime example, `gfortran` prints error at the compilation stage itself since the length of the string is available at compile-time:

```console
% cat examples/expr2.f90 
program main
    character(5):: x = "Hello"
    print*, iachar(x)
 end
% gfortran examples/expr2.f90
examples/expr2.f90:3:19:

    3 |     print*, iachar(x)
      |                   1
Error: Argument of iachar at (1) must be of length one
```

When the length of the string is not available at compile-time, for example when the string is an allocatable string:

```console
% cat examples/expr2.f90     
program main
    character(len=:), allocatable:: x
    allocate(character(len=10) :: x)
    x = "Bat"
    print*, iachar(x)
end
% gfortran examples/expr2.f90
% ./a.out 
          66
```

`gfortran` does not seem to print any error. Instead it seems to simply use the first character of the allocatable string.

Second:

Removed unused/old intrinsic code here https://github.com/lfortran/lfortran/pull/4075. Now you have `ichar` implemented as an intrinsic registry function and `iachar` implemented at the ASR level in `ast_common_visitor`. 

Adding checks for `iachar` might be straigthforward as it currently implemented in AST->ASR. Also, checking length for compile-time argument length should be straightforward for registry functions and can be done in the `eval_*()` (For example `eval_Ichar()`) function.

Now considering the case of checking for runtime-time argument with compile-time length. I think for this we need to add support in the generator script. We recently updated the script to support checking for `complex64` (complex of kind 8) here https://github.com/lfortran/lfortran/pull/3955#discussion_r1596121132. I think you can similarly define

```c++
template <int32_t length>
static inline bool is_character(ASR::ttype_t &x) {
    if (is_character(x)) {
        // check if length is < 0 which means length is not available at compile-time
        // if length is not available simply return true (gfortran seems to work with runtime length)

        // if length >= 0 which means length is available at compile-time
        return compile_time_length == length;
    }
    return false;
}
```

The only concern I have with the above is it would detect runtime-args with compile-time lengths not equal to `1`, but it might not be able to produce a very descriptive error. We might need to think/investigate how to print a good/descriptive error for this. #4015 

Use `fgets()` to read `n` characters from `stdin` where `n` is the length of the variable which will store the data. When reading from a file, we follow the same logic using the `fread()` function.
 
### Console read
```fortran
program main
    character(len=2) :: c
    read *, c
    print *, c
    print*, len(c)
end
```
#### Output on main
```console
apple
5
```
#### Output on branch
```console
ap
2
```

### File read
```fortran
program hello
    character(3) :: c
    open(11, file="hello.txt", form="formatted", access="stream", status="old")
    read(11, *) c
    print *, c
    print *, len(c)
end program
```
Content of `hello.txt` is
```
Hello

```
#### Output on main
```console
Hello
5
```
#### Output on branch
```console
Hel
3
